statements.label: not_addressed
statements.text: The ANTSR locus controls female development by regulating sex-specific splicing of the transformer gene.
statements.evidence: These findings demonstrate that an essential noncoding locus can retain its function over deep evolutionary time without sequence conservation.
statements.note: The abstract identifies ANTSR as the primary female-determining signal but names no downstream target gene or splicing mechanism.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: For a span exceeding 150 million years, the multiallelic noncoding ANTSR locus has remained the main trigger of female development in aculeate Hymenoptera.
statements.evidence: we reveal that the ANTSR locus, a multiallelic noncoding locus, has been maintained for over 150 My as the primary instructive signal for female development
statements.note: The abstract states that the noncoding ANTSR locus has served as the primary instructive signal for female development for over 150 My.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: The ANTSR locus sits in a conserved synteny block dating to the origin of Aculeata, and only individuals heterozygous at it develop as females.
statements.evidence: This locus is located in a conserved synteny block that originated at the base of Aculeata and functions as a highly polymorphic, zygosity-based sex determiner, with only heterozygous individuals developing as females across lineages.
statements.note: The abstract places the locus in a conserved synteny block that originated at the base of Aculeata and says only heterozygotes become females.

statements.label: supported
statements.text: Even though its role is ancient, the ANTSR sex locus shows no recognisable sequence similarity between the lineages compared.
statements.evidence: Despite its deep evolutionary conservation, this sex locus shows no detectable sequence homology among lineages.
statements.note: The abstract reports no detectable sequence homology of the sex locus among lineages despite its deep evolutionary conservation.

statements.label: supported

statements.note: The abstract reports a new vertebrate MRF type and an inferred ancestral two-gene state matching the early- and late-acting MRF types.

statements.text: Synteny shared among chordate MRF loci indicates that the two vertebrate whole-genome duplications were a major force in vertebrate MRF evolution.

statements.note: The abstract states that conserved synteny between chordate MRF loci supports the 2R WGD events as a major force in vertebrate MRF evolution.
